en: The Śalya Parva (The Book of the Spear)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jayam).
Thus, when Karṇa had been slain by Kirīṭin as Jambha was by Indra,
Saṃjaya returned and reported the battle once more to the king.
O King, when Vaikartana— the crest-jewel of all heroes, a wish-fulfilling tree for those who seek his aid, and one who turned every hope into night— was slain, [the world was plunged in darkness].
When he had departed for some unknown place, Duryodhana, distressed as if his own life-force had left him, felt breathless and perceived the ten directions as empty.
Ready to fight the Pāṇḍavas, he moved in the midst of the chariot-warriors; though his body remained the same, he was like a man who has already departed for the next world.
Then, having appointed Śalya as the commander-in-chief at the word of the son of Droṇa,
the king entered the abode of the gods for the sake of his kingdom, leaving the battle behind.
There were more than ten thousand chariots, as many elephants, two hundred thousand horses, and thirty million foot soldiers.
This was the remainder of the army of the Kuru king in the battle;
and half of the force of the Pāṇḍavas likewise remained as the survivors after being slain.
In this terrible battlefield, a circle of destruction for kings, where foot soldiers,
chariots, and elephants wallowed in the mire of brains.
The lotus of his face was strewn about; his chariot-wheels were shattered by the impact of the colors;
the mass of royal elephants was cast down; and the ground was thick with the blue lotuses of severed sword-blades.
It was as if a lake had been churned by an untimely black elephant, leaving behind only the moss of hair, the mud of filth, and the slush of mucus.
In that forest, where the ears of excellent horses lay fallen as marks, which was covered with broken bows, and where the plantain trunks were tossed about as if struck by thunderbolts; Bhmj_9.12.
In that place, which was like the garden of Time, filled with skulls for drinking cups and stirred by the potent liquor of manifest power, full of the parts of blue lotuses; Bhmj_9.13.
When the battle had begun once more, Śalya, the son of Hṛdika, and the son of Subala,
along with Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, and Suyodhana, entered the Pāṇḍava army.
Pārtha, Pārṣata, Śaineya, the sons of Draupadī, and Śikhaṇḍin struck down the armies of the Trigartas, Gāndhāras, and the Kapi lord.
In that battle without restraint, the great chariot-warriors, like men intoxicated,
fought fiercely in their wrath, having lost their kinsmen and circles of friends.
Nakula slew the heroes Satyasena, Suṣeṇa, and Citrasena, the sons of Karṇa, whose prowess was equal to that of Karṇa himself.
Then, being crushed by the mighty Śalya like a lotus-pond by an elephant,
the Pandava army trembled with a great roar.
Seeing his army being struck down by Śalya, that thorn among enemies, Bhīma, mace in hand and filled with fierce rage, rushed toward him.
Having destroyed the chariot of him who could shatter hundreds of chariots with his mace,
he stood before the one who was about to die, like Death himself with staff raised.
Taking up his mace adorned with golden bands, the King of Madra,
possessed of terrible strength, fought Bhīma in anger, arrogant with pride.
Moving in circles, they both lunged at one another and struck with their maces, from which sparks were produced by the impact.
When those two had quickly fainted and fallen to the ground from their stupor,
the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, along with their followers, arrived swiftly and in great agitation.
Having suddenly regained consciousness, while the two of them remained as they were,
the heroes headed by Duryodhana fought with the leaders of the Pārthas.
While the kings were fighting, desiring the world of Brahmā,
Suyodhana slew Cekitāna, the best among monarchs.
Then the King of Madra, enraged, single-handedly held back the sons of Pāṇḍu along with their followers by force, while being honored by the sky-dwellers.
Having cut down that shower of weapons discharged by him with his own arrows without any agitation,
Śalya in an instant rendered those [enemies] invisible with his feathered shafts.
When his army was shrouded by a net of arrows by the King of Madra,
the son of Dharma, filled with rage, destroyed two thousand chariots.
Seeing his followers slain by the king in battle, Śalya then made Yudhiṣṭhira appear like a full Ashoka tree with hundreds of stone-tipped arrows.
When the son of Dharma was thus afflicted, Nakula, trembling with rage,
along with Bhīma, Sātyaki, and the other leaders, covered Śalya with a shower of arrows.
Then Śalya, shrouding the interior of the world with a darkness of arrows and producing a roar like a thundercloud, crushed Pārtha’s army.
Agitated in that battle, Jishnu fought Drona;
Bhimasena fought Duryodhana, and Nakula fought the son of Subala.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, having destroyed all the weapons of Śalya, whose enemies had been entirely exhausted, cut his chariot into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
Mounting another chariot, the King of Madra, blazing with rage, deprived the son of Dharma of his bow, chariot, and banner.
Then Bhīmasena, seeing the king deprived of his chariot,
became agitated and shattered the chariot of the King of Madra along with all its weapons.
Then Śalya, sword in hand, moving with the prowess of Garuḍa, roamed about with his body unobserved, slaughtering chariots and elephants.
Then [he saw her] veiled by a flaming red silk scarf,
radiant with inlaid jewels, like a row of the teeth of Death.
"This is the end of the Kuru army; whence could there be such a battle?"—thus, as if crying out with masses of bells, she roared like a thunderclap.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the best among the powerful, possessing the prowess of six-faced Kārttikeya, hurled a blazing spear capable of slaying a thousand at the King of Madra.
With his heart pierced by her, that best of kings fell down,
with torrents of blood flowing from the openings of his ears, nose, and mouth.
***** The Slaying of Śalya // 1 // ***** When Śalya— the remaining support for the hopes of the Kauravas— was slain, all the chariot-warriors fled, their pride and aspirations shattered. Bhmj_9.41 //
Then Śalya’s younger brother, named Vicitrakavaca, filled with rage,
advanced against Dharmarāja as he was tearing through the army.
The son of Dharma severed his head, which was radiant with various jewels, just as one might cut off a lofty peak of Mount Rohaṇa, while he was raining down arrows.
When he was slain,
Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, and the son of Hṛdika quickly turned back and approached the banner-bearing army as it broke apart, leaderless.
As the Cedis and Pañcālas, having found their mark,
raised their shouts, those great car-warriors fought for a moment as if they had multiplied into many.
Then, out of indignation at the slaughter of his master, he rushed against Yudhiṣṭhira;
having slain the remaining Madras, he indeed made the earth free of Madras.
Then Bhīma, mace in hand and skilled in the art of destruction,
crushed all the Mlecchas and made the battlefield as if empty.
Then, when the heroic Satyaki had struck down Satyarāja,
Duryodhana himself approached and fought against the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Among the Pāṇḍavas there was neither chariot, nor elephant, nor horse,
nor warrior that was not covered by the arrows of Duryodhana, marked with the name of Hema.
The herd of elephants trembled before him as he rained down iron arrows,
repeatedly struck by the sharp sounds of his bowstring and the clanging of jewels and gold.
While Duryodhana was fighting, his enemies having found their mark, the sons of Droṇa, the son of Hṛdika, Suśarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Subala arrived.
In that terrible conflict, as those warriors struck with relentless force,
the world became shrouded in darkness when the sun was obscured by the rising dust.
When the unbearable dust, capable of striking down the lordly elephants,
arose, no distinction whatsoever could be made, as if the dissolution of a kalpa had arrived.
"Where is the son of Droṇa? Where is the king of Gāndhāra? And where is King Suyodhana?"—such was the great clamor that arose everywhere among the Pāṇḍava armies.
At that moment, when the field of vision was overtaken by the whirlpools of dissolution,
the son of the Wind-god struck down the remaining younger brothers of Duryodhana.
Having slain Mahābāhu, Bhūribala, Jaitra, Durdarśana, Śala, and Sunāda— all of whom were destined for destruction— he uttered a great roar.
Then the hero Sātyaki seized me in that incomparable battle, saying with agitation, "This is Sañjaya, captured by me! (Bhājana 9.57)
Then Arjuna, having slain Suśarman along with his sons and his followers,
completely destroyed the army of the Saṃśaptakas with his arrows.
In that gambling match called battle, Sahadeva, repeatedly casting the dice of arrows,
struck off Śakuni’s head with a crescent-headed shaft.

***** The Slaying of the Bird (Śakuni) ***** Having slain the owl and its offspring, the son of Mādrī, remembering the period of his forest exile, struck down the army of the Gāndhāras. (Bhājana 9.60)
Then, when his army had been completely destroyed, King Suyodhana, exhausted and deprived of his mounts,
withdrew from the battlefield and fled on foot.
When that great battle had ended in an instant, leaving only Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa, the assembly of spirits and *vetālas* was entirely destroyed.
When the grandson of Śini was prepared to strike me down at the word of Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
the Blessed Vyāsa, a treasury of compassion, protected him.
Then, at the end of the day, afflicted with grief, I set out for Suyodhana; I beheld the cakravartin, whose heart was as firm as a diamond, departing.
Seeing me on foot, his neck bent low with shame, he said to King Sañjaya, "You should say this to my father: BhmJ 9.65.
Deprived of that friend Karṇa and those heroes,
including Duḥśāsana and the others, your son has entered the lake, bereft of them all.
Having said "Me," and having solidified the water through his demonic power (*daityamāyā*),
he entered the vast lake, overwhelmed by the fire of intense grief.
Knowing that he had entered the lake where the water was solidified by his pillar-like thighs, Kṛpa— the son of my preceptor—
and King Bhoja, whose feet were kissed by the crest-jewels of monarchs and who was the abode of the play of Fortune, approached him and lamented.

Then, surrounded by an *akṣauhiṇī* of troops, the son of Dharma abandoned his home at night along with all the royal ladies and Yuyutsu; together with Dhanañjaya, Bhīma, and the other leaders, he set his mind upon Duryodhana as if he were a remaining debt.

He upon whose head the garlands of moonbeams from the toenails of his lotus-feet shone like actual garlands upon the heads of kings—he, that very son of the Kuru king, has now gone forth on foot! Fie upon destiny, which blooms with transient splendor!
Salutations ever to that Destiny, by whose power, alas, the cycles of phenomena— possessing highs and lows, prone to dissolution, and sealed by the delusions of ascetics— enter into a state of ruin.
Thus ends the Śalyaparvan in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Kṣemendra.
